message.content:
The earliest non‑biblical references to Jesus come from Roman and Jewish writers who lived within a few decades of his death.

| Author | Work | Date | Reference |
|--------|------|------|-----------|
| **Flavius Josephus** | *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3) | c. 93–94 CE | “...the wise man was called Jesus…he was crucified by Pontius Pilate…” |
| **Tacitus** | *Annals* (Book 15, Chapter 44) | c. 116 CE | “Christus, the founder of the name, was executed under Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.” |
| **Pliny the Younger** | Letter to Emperor Trajan (Letter 10.96) | c. 112 CE | Mentions early Christians worshipping “Christ” as a god. |

Josephus’s passage is the earliest surviving text that explicitly names Jesus and places him in the historical context of the first century. It is dated to the late 90s CE, roughly 30–40 years after Jesus’s supposed crucifixion. Tacitus’s account, written about 20 years later, corroborates the crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. These two independent sources are generally accepted by scholars as the earliest reliable historical references to Jesus outside the New Testament.
